contents.text: If you don't know the meaning of a word, you can look for context clues. Context clues are nearby words and phrases that help you figure out the meaning of an unknown word.

header.text: Here are some examples:

sentences.text: Maureen asked for expedited service for her passport so that she'd have it in time for her trip.
You can guess that expedited means "hurried or sped up."
At the city council meeting, Mr. Harrington lambasted the mayor for refusing to address the city's traffic problem.
You can guess that lambasted means "criticized or verbally attacked."
Nobody understood why Corey decided to move to France. His decision to go there seemed completely arbitrary.
You can guess that arbitrary means "random."

header.text: Voracious means having a huge appetite. The context clue Every day, it eats its entire body weight in prey helps you figure out the meaning.

contents.text: The shrew is a tiny, mouse-like mammal with an elevated metabolic rate. In the space of just one minute, it breathes about eight hundred times, and its heart beats about one thousand times. The shrew is also voracious. Every day, it eats its entire body weight in prey such as insects, worms, and salamanders.

contents.text: Which of these professions do you think requires more formal education—being a lawyer or being a college professor?
There are four kinds of sentences.

header.text: A declarative sentence is a statement, and it always ends with a period.

contents.text: The nurse told Mr. Abrams to roll up his sleeve so that she could check his blood pressure.

header.text: An interrogative sentence is a question, and it always ends with a question mark.

contents.text: Do you have any plans for the upcoming weekend?

header.text: An imperative sentence is a command. It makes a request or tells someone to do something, and it usually ends with a period. If the command shows strong feeling, it ends with an exclamation point.

sentences.text: For this assignment, use references to support your claims.
Don't drive so quickly in the construction zone!

header.text: An exclamatory sentence is like a statement, but it shows surprise or strong feeling. An exclamatory sentence always ends with an exclamation point.

contents.text: I can't wait to travel through Europe this summer!

content.text: The sentence asks something, and it ends with a question mark. It is an interrogative sentence.

lessons.name: Identify the simple subject or simple predicate of a sentence

header.text: Select the simple subject.

contents.text: Every sentence has a subject and a predicate.

header.text: The simple subject tells who or what is doing something. It is just the subject noun or pronoun without any other words that describe or modify it.

sentences.text: Jennifer sleeps late on the weekends.
Her best friend sleeps late on the weekends.
Mrs. Peterson sleeps late on the weekends.

contents.text: The simple subject tells who sleeps late on the weekends.

header.text: The simple predicate tells what the subject is doing. It is just the verb without any other words that describe or modify it.

sentences.text: Her best friend sleeps.
Her best friend sleeps late on the weekends.

contents.text: The simple predicate tells what her best friend does.

textContent.text: Fern came almost every day to visit him.…Here she sat quietly during the long afternoons, thinking and listening and watching Wilbur. The sheep soon got to know her and trust her. So did the geese, who lived with the sheep. All the animals trusted her, she was so quiet and friendly.…It made her happy just to be near the pig, and it made Wilbur happy to know that she was sitting there, right outside his pen.
From E. B. White, Charlotte's Web. Copyright 1952 by E. B. White

contents.text: Figures of speech are words or phrases that use language in a nonliteral or unusual way.

header.text: An allusion is a brief reference to something or someone well known, often from history or literature.

sentences.text: So Eden sank to grief,
So dawn goes down to day.
Nothing gold can stay.
—Robert Frost, "Nothing Gold Can Stay"

header.text: Hyperbole is an obvious exaggeration that is not meant to be taken literally.

sentences.text: There did not seem to be brains enough in the entire nursery, so to speak, to bait a fish-hook with.
—Mark Twain, A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court

header.text: Personification is giving human characteristics to nonhuman things.

sentences.text: April is the cruellest month.
—T. S. Eliot, "The Waste Land"

header.text: A simile uses like or as to compare two things.

sentences.text: No, no, we are not satisfied and will not be satisfied until justice rolls down like water and righteousness like a mighty stream.
—Martin Luther King, Jr., "I Have a Dream"

header.text: A metaphor compares two things that are not actually alike without using like or as.

sentences.text: But, soft! what light through yonder window breaks?
It is the east, and Juliet is the sun.
—William Shakespeare, Romeo and Juliet

header.text: Verbal irony involves saying one thing but actually meaning something very different. People often use verbal irony when they are being sarcastic.

sentences.text: Thirty-five is a very attractive age. London society is full of women of the very highest birth who have, of their own free choice, remained thirty-five for years.
—Oscar Wilde, The Importance of Being Earnest

content.text: The narrator compares his mother to a commando unit, using like. This is a simile.

header.text: <instructions>Review the passage. The simile is shown in bold.</instructions>

contents.text: My mom sighs. "We can't do this without you. Being around kids is good for Natalie." …

My mom is like a one-woman commando unit. She could win land battles, air battles, water battles, outer space battles too, probably. I wonder if there would be time to get Natalie and then get back to school in time to play ball with the guys. It would be embarrassing to have her there, but at least I could play.
<citation>From Gennifer Choldenko, Al Capone Does My Shirts. Copyright 2004 by Gennifer Choldenko</citation>
<instructions>What is the effect of the simile on the passage's meaning or tone?</instructions>

choices.text: It suggests that the narrator's mother is lonely.
It suggests that the narrator's mother is persuasive.

contents.text: Figures of speech can contribute to a passage's meaning or tone.

header.text: An allusion draws on meanings and characteristics associated with the original source.

contents.text: Frost makes a reference to the biblical Garden of Eden to emphasize a sense of loss.

header.text: Hyperbole can be used to emphasize strong emotions or sometimes for the sake of comedy.

contents.text: Twain's narrator states that "there did not seem to be brains enough…to bait a fish-hook with" to express that the people of Camelot were unintelligent, not that they literally had a small quantity of brains.

header.text: Personification makes readers think about animals, non-human objects, or ideas in an emotional, relatable, or sympathetic way.

contents.text: By calling April "the cruellest month," Eliot illustrates the resentment and sorrow he feels at the coming of spring.

header.text: A simile can affect the meaning or tone of a passage by providing a vivid image.

contents.text: Dr. King compares justice to water and righteousness to "a mighty stream" in order to give his speech an urgent tone.

header.text: A metaphor adds creative and vivid imagery to a passage.

contents.text: By comparing Juliet to the sun, Shakespeare shows how Romeo idealizes Juliet.

header.text: Verbal irony often implies something very different from what has been directly stated.

contents.text: The claim that many women have "remained thirty-five for years" is clearly not factually true, but Wilde uses it to humorously suggest that some older women will not admit their true ages.

choices.text: It suggests that the narrator's mother is lonely.
It suggests that the narrator's mother is persuasive.

content.text: The simile suggests that the narrator's mother is persuasive. The narrator compares his mother to a one-woman commando unit to suggest that she is good at winning arguments.

contents.text: Ann-Margret brought George Burns along to see Peter perform. George Burns was older than the century, older than time.

To Peter, George's date with Ann-Margret represented Hollywood's last gasp of glamour. The star of Kitten With a Whip also liked Peter. "I remember someone had said something about me," Ann-Margret would explain in her Hollywood-mystic whisper, "and he got after that person. And I said thank you for standing up for me."
<citation>From Stephen MacLean, Peter Allen: The Boy from Oz. Copyright 1996 by Stephen MacLean</citation>

contents.text: "Aline!"
Aline, ugly, neat and enigmatic, appeared with the breakfast-tray. A delicious scent preceded her.
Mrs. Clephane raised herself on a pink elbow, shook her hair over her shoulders, and exclaimed: "Violets?"
Aline permitted herself her dry smile. "From a gentleman."

Color flooded her mistress's face. Hadn't she known that something good was going to happen to her that morning—hadn't she felt it in every touch of the sunshine, as its golden fingertips pressed her lids open and wound their way through her hair? She supposed she was superstitious. She laughed expectantly.
<citation>From Edith Wharton, The Mother's Recompense. Copyright 1925 by Edith Wharton</citation>

contents.text: To make your writing more interesting, try to use a mix of different kinds of sentences. You can get ideas for new kinds of sentences by imitating sentences that you read.

To imitate a model sentence, first look at its form, or pattern. Ask what sorts of words, phrases, and clauses the sentence uses and what order they are in. Then, create a new sentence following the same pattern.

header.text: Model sentence:

sentences.text: When I stepped out into the bright sunlight from the darkness of the movie house, I had only two things on my mind: Paul Newman and a ride home.
—S. E. Hinton, The Outsiders. © 1967

header.text: New sentence:

contents.text: As long as our secret hideout stayed hidden from other people in the deep, deserted forest, we would have our lifelong dream: no parents and plenty of beef jerky.
Both sentences use a subordinating conjunction (when and as long as) to introduce the first clause.
Both sentences use prepositional phrases (into the bright sunlight; from the darkness of the movie house; from other people; and in the deep, deserted forest) to modify parts of the first clause.
Both sentences use a colon (:) to introduce final noun phrases (Paul Newman and a ride home and no parents and plenty of beef jerky).

contents.text: To make your writing more interesting, try to use a mix of different kinds of sentences. You can get ideas for new kinds of sentences by imitating sentences that you read.

To imitate a model sentence, first look at its form, or pattern. Ask what sorts of words, phrases, and clauses the sentence uses and what order they are in. Then, create a new sentence following the same pattern.

header.text: Model sentence:

sentences.text: When I stepped out into the bright sunlight from the darkness of the movie house, I had only two things on my mind: Paul Newman and a ride home.
—S. E. Hinton, The Outsiders. © 1967

header.text: New sentence:

contents.text: As long as our secret hideout stayed hidden from other people in the deep, deserted forest, we would have our lifelong dream: no parents and plenty of beef jerky.
Both sentences use a subordinating conjunction (when and as long as) to introduce the first clause.
Both sentences use prepositional phrases (into the bright sunlight; from the darkness of the movie house; from other people; and in the deep, deserted forest) to modify parts of the first clause.
Both sentences use a colon (:) to introduce final noun phrases (Paul Newman and a ride home and no parents and plenty of beef jerky).
